Akkadian Empire.summary: Sargon’s dynasty united Mesopotamian cities and extended royal control into neighboring regions, creating an early territorial empire.
Akkadian Empire.capital: Akkad (Agade); its archaeological location has not been identified.
Akkadian Empire.economy: Royal centralization accompanied more standardized weights, measures, calendars and administrative archives.
Akkadian Empire.military: Successive conquests brought Mesopotamian city-states and neighboring territories under Akkadian kings.
Akkadian Empire.contributions: Standardized administrative practices and cuneiform writing across a large territorial state.
Akkadian Empire.origin: Sargon consolidated previously separate Mesopotamian city-states under his dynasty.
Akkadian Empire.periodNote: 2334–2154 BCE follows the University of Chicago museum chronology; absolute dates and the empire’s final decades remain debated.

sources.title: Akkadian period (2334–2154 BC) — University of Chicago

Neo-Assyrian Empire.summary: A northern Mesopotamian empire that expanded through conquest, provincial administration, tribute and forced population transfers.
Neo-Assyrian Empire.capital: Ashur; Kalhu under Ashurnasirpal II; Dur-Sharrukin under Sargon II; Nineveh under Sennacherib and his successors.
Neo-Assyrian Empire.rulers: Selected rulers: Ashurnasirpal II, 883–859 BCE; Sennacherib, 704–681 BCE; Ashurbanipal, 668–627 BCE.
Neo-Assyrian Empire.economy: Tribute and war booty flowed from conquered regions into Assyria’s capitals.
Neo-Assyrian Empire.military: Armies conducted sieges and cavalry campaigns across the Near East; conquered regions supplied tribute and were governed or subordinated to Assyria.
Neo-Assyrian Empire.contributions: Monumental palace reliefs, royal archives and Ashurbanipal’s collection preserved major works of Mesopotamian literature and scholarship.
Neo-Assyrian Empire.origin: Assyrian kings renewed territorial expansion from northern Mesopotamia during the early first millennium BCE.
Neo-Assyrian Empire.decline: Babylonian and Median forces destroyed Nineveh in 612 BCE; Assyrian resistance continued afterward.
Neo-Assyrian Empire.periodNote: 612 BCE marks Nineveh’s fall, not the instantaneous end of every Assyrian force; sources use later endpoints for the remaining resistance.

Achaemenid Empire.summary: A Persian imperial monarchy joining territories from the eastern Mediterranean to Central and South Asia through satrapal government.
Achaemenid Empire.capital: Pasargadae under Cyrus; Susa and Persepolis developed under Darius I. The court used multiple royal centers.
Achaemenid Empire.currency: Gold daric and silver siglos; regional currencies also circulated.
Achaemenid Empire.rulers: Selected rulers: Cyrus II, 559–530 BCE; Darius I, 522–486 BCE; Xerxes I, 486–465 BCE.
Achaemenid Empire.economy: Provincial tribute and long-distance communications supported a monarchy governing diverse regional economies.
Achaemenid Empire.military: Conquest incorporated Lydia, Babylonia and Egypt; campaigns against mainland Greek states encountered major defeats.
Achaemenid Empire.contributions: Satrapal administration, imperial roads and monumental architecture connected diverse peoples across a large state.
Achaemenid Empire.origin: Cyrus defeated the Median king Astyages in 550 BCE, then conquered neighboring kingdoms.
Achaemenid Empire.decline: Alexander defeated Persian armies and seized provinces; Darius III was killed in 330 BCE.
Achaemenid Empire.periodNote: 550 BCE marks Cyrus’s conquest of Media. Sources sometimes use 331 BCE, the battle of Gaugamela, rather than Darius III’s death in 330.

Empire of Alexander the Great.summary: Alexander’s Macedonian monarchy conquered the Achaemenid realm, linking Greece, Egypt and western Asia before fragmenting after his death.
Empire of Alexander the Great.currency: Silver drachm-based coinage, including tetradrachms issued in Alexander’s name.
Empire of Alexander the Great.military: Campaigns from 334 to 323 BCE carried Macedonian armies through the Persian Empire to northwestern South Asia.
Empire of Alexander the Great.contributions: Conquest accelerated exchanges between Greek and other cultures that shaped the subsequent Hellenistic kingdoms.
Empire of Alexander the Great.origin: Alexander inherited Macedonia’s throne in 336 BCE and launched the invasion of Persian territory in 334 BCE.
Empire of Alexander the Great.decline: After Alexander died in 323 BCE, rival generals fought over and divided his territories.
Empire of Alexander the Great.periodNote: Dates describe Alexander’s reign; the Asian conquests began in 334 BCE, and successor governments persisted after his death.

Roman Republic.summary: A Roman state governed through magistrates, assemblies and a powerful Senate that acquired an extensive Mediterranean empire before civil wars transformed its government.
Roman Republic.currency: Bronze, silver and gold coinages, with the denarius a major silver denomination in the later Republic.
Roman Republic.rulers: Selected officeholder: Marcus Tullius Cicero, consul in 63 BCE. Republican authority was shared among magistrates and the Senate.
Roman Republic.economy: Conquest brought land, wealth and enslaved people into an agrarian state; the distribution of imperial gains intensified social conflict.
Roman Republic.military: Citizen armies and allied forces expanded Roman control; successful generals increasingly turned military power against domestic rivals.
Roman Republic.contributions: Republican magistracies, assemblies, law and military roads became influential institutional and infrastructural precedents.
Roman Republic.origin: Tradition dates the expulsion of Rome’s last king and establishment of the Republic to 509 BCE.
Roman Republic.decline: Civil wars, concentrated military power and political violence culminated in Octavian’s supremacy and the Augustan settlement of 27 BCE.
Roman Republic.periodNote: 509 BCE is the traditional foundation date. Rome already possessed an empire while its constitutional government remained republican.

sources.title: Roman Art: A Resource for Educators — The Met

Roman Empire.summary: Rome’s imperial government dominated the Mediterranean world; its eastern continuation survived long after the western imperial office ended.
Roman Empire.capital: Rome initially; later imperial residences multiplied. Constantinople became a new imperial capital in 330 CE.
Roman Empire.currency: Gold aureus, silver denarius and bronze denominations in the early empire; later monetary systems changed.
Roman Empire.rulers: Selected rulers: Augustus, 27 BCE–14 CE; Constantine I, 306–337 CE.
Roman Empire.economy: Roads and sea routes circulated agricultural produce, people and other commodities across connected Mediterranean provinces.
Roman Empire.military: Imperial authority rested on extensive military power; conquest joined regions around the Mediterranean under Roman rule.
Roman Empire.contributions: Connected transport networks, urban architecture and Roman legal traditions shaped later Mediterranean and European societies.
Roman Empire.origin: Augustus established predominant personal authority after the late Republic’s civil wars.
Roman Empire.decline: The western emperor Romulus Augustus was deposed in 476; eastern Roman government continued from Constantinople.
Roman Empire.periodNote: 476 CE is a conventional western endpoint. This record overlaps the Byzantine record because Byzantium was the eastern Roman continuation, not an unrelated new civilization.

Byzantine Empire.summary: The Roman state centered on Constantinople, whose inhabitants called themselves Romans; its language, territory and institutions changed across more than a millennium.
Byzantine Empire.capital: Constantinople, except during the Latin occupation of 1204–1261, when rival Roman successor courts operated elsewhere.
Byzantine Empire.currency: Gold solidus in the early Byzantine period; coinage changed substantially over later centuries.
Byzantine Empire.rulers: Selected rulers: Constantine I, 306–337; Justinian I, 527–565.
Byzantine Empire.economy: Constantinople occupied a major intersection of east–west trade; taxes and army payments used imperial coinage.
Byzantine Empire.military: Justinian recovered western territories, but subsequent Persian, Arab, Latin and Turkish advances reduced imperial control.
Byzantine Empire.contributions: Preserved and transformed Roman law, Greek learning, Christian architecture, mosaics and manuscript traditions.
Byzantine Empire.origin: Constantine inaugurated Constantinople in 330; eastern Roman institutions continued through the collapse of western imperial government.
Byzantine Empire.decline: The Fourth Crusade fractured the empire in 1204; after restoration, a diminished state ended with the Ottoman capture of Constantinople in 1453.
Byzantine Empire.periodNote: 330 is a conventional starting point, not a declaration of a new Byzantine state. The Latin occupation interrupted Constantinople-based rule in 1204–1261.

Rashidun Caliphate.summary: The polity led by the first four caliphs after Muhammad’s death expanded from Arabia into Byzantine and Sasanian territories.
Rashidun Caliphate.capital: Medina initially; Kufa under Ali, who ruled in 656–661.
Rashidun Caliphate.rulers: Selected rulers: Umar ibn al-Khattab, 634–644; Ali ibn Abi Talib, 656–661.
Rashidun Caliphate.military: Arab armies conquered territories including Egypt, Syria and Iraq, taking advantage of weakened Byzantine and Sasanian power.
Rashidun Caliphate.contributions: Established the first caliphal governments outside Arabia and founded Fustat as an administrative center in Egypt.
Rashidun Caliphate.origin: Leadership of the Muslim community passed to caliphs following Muhammad’s death in 632.
Rashidun Caliphate.decline: Civil conflict and Ali’s assassination preceded Muawiya’s establishment of Umayyad dynastic rule in 661.
Rashidun Caliphate.periodNote: The conventional period ends in 661; succession and legitimacy were contested, and “Rightly Guided” is a traditional designation.

Kufa — Encyclopaedia Iranica

Umayyad Caliphate.summary: A dynastic caliphate centered on Damascus that expanded from the Atlantic region to the Indus Valley.
Umayyad Caliphate.capital: Damascus for most of the period; this entry does not include the later Umayyad state in Iberia.
Umayyad Caliphate.currency: Gold dinar and silver dirham, including the epigraphic coinage developed under Abd al-Malik.
Umayyad Caliphate.rulers: Selected rulers: Muawiya I, 661–680; Abd al-Malik, 685–705; al-Walid I, 705–715.
Umayyad Caliphate.economy: Unified coinage and administrative institutions strengthened central rule across diverse provincial economies.
Umayyad Caliphate.military: Successive conquests expanded caliphal territory across North Africa and into Iberia and South Asia.
Umayyad Caliphate.contributions: Arabic administration, reformed coinage and monuments including the Dome of the Rock helped shape early Islamic institutional and artistic traditions.
Umayyad Caliphate.origin: Muawiya established dynastic authority after the first civil war and Ali’s assassination.
Umayyad Caliphate.decline: The Abbasids replaced Umayyad rule in 750; a separate Umayyad dynasty later ruled in Iberia.
Umayyad Caliphate.periodNote: 661–750 describes the Damascus-based caliphate, not the later emirate and caliphate of Córdoba.

Abbasid Caliphate.summary: A caliphate centered in Iraq whose initial political empire later fragmented while Abbasid caliphs retained varying degrees of religious and regional authority.
Abbasid Caliphate.capital: Baghdad from 762; Samarra served as the principal capital in 836–892.
Abbasid Caliphate.currency: Gold dinars and silver dirhams; issues varied across periods and mints.
Abbasid Caliphate.economy: Baghdad and Samarra became important commercial and cultural centers connecting regional economies.
Abbasid Caliphate.military: Al-Mutasim established Samarra to accommodate an army including Turkish slave soldiers; later dynasties exercised much of the caliphate’s effective military authority.
Abbasid Caliphate.contributions: Patronage of scholarship, urban architecture and ceramic techniques had a lasting influence across the Islamic world.
Abbasid Caliphate.origin: The Abbasid dynasty replaced the Umayyads in 750 and shifted the political center from Syria to Iraq.
Abbasid Caliphate.decline: Provincial autonomy and military dynasties eroded central power; Mongol forces sacked Baghdad in 1258.
Abbasid Caliphate.periodNote: 1258 ends the Baghdad caliphate. Later Abbasid caliphs in Mamluk Cairo held primarily nominal authority; caliphal claims do not equal continuous territorial control.

Ottoman Empire.summary: A dynastic empire originating in northwestern Anatolia that governed diverse societies across southeastern Europe, western Asia and North Africa.
Ottoman Empire.capital: Bursa and Edirne preceded Constantinople/Istanbul, the imperial center after its conquest in 1453.
Ottoman Empire.currency: Silver akçe and copper coins initially; gold sultani from the late fifteenth century; kuruş and lira systems in later periods.
Ottoman Empire.economy: Agriculture and commercial centers supported imperial society; Bursa’s bazaars and rural foundations illustrate the connection between trade, production and public institutions.
Ottoman Empire.military: Under Suleiman, Ottoman forces expanded into southeastern Europe and Iraq while competing with the Habsburg and Safavid states.
Ottoman Empire.contributions: Imperial architecture, court arts and legal institutions shaped societies across former Ottoman territories.
Ottoman Empire.origin: Osman’s Anatolian principality expanded through warfare and alliances into a territorial state.
Ottoman Empire.decline: Territorial losses and defeat in the First World War ended imperial power; the sultanate was abolished before the Turkish republic’s establishment.
Ottoman Empire.periodNote: 1299 is a conventional foundation date. The sultanate ended in 1922; the republic began in 1923 and the caliphate was abolished in 1924.

Spanish Empire.summary: A composite monarchy and overseas colonial system connecting American, European, African and Asian territories through conquest, settlement and regulated trade.
Spanish Empire.capital: Madrid from 1561; the royal court moved to Valladolid in 1601–1606.
Spanish Empire.currency: Silver peso of eight reales was a major international trade coin; other currencies varied by territory and period.
Spanish Empire.economy: American silver, export agriculture and regulated shipping sustained imperial revenues; forced labor and slavery were integral to colonial production.
Spanish Empire.military: Armed Atlantic convoys protected bullion shipments; colonial conquest depended on Spanish forces and Indigenous allies.
Spanish Empire.contributions: Transatlantic and transpacific routes connected world trade; colonial rule also caused dispossession, coerced labor and profound demographic loss.
Spanish Empire.origin: Crown-sponsored Atlantic voyages and conquest established American colonies, followed by expansion across the Pacific.
Spanish Empire.decline: American independence movements dismantled most mainland rule; later decolonization reduced overseas possessions, including Spain’s withdrawal from Western Sahara in 1976.
Spanish Empire.periodNote: 1492–1976 is an overseas-imperial convention. The final date marks Spain’s withdrawal from Western Sahara, whose status remained unresolved; it is not a universal endpoint for all Spanish overseas possessions.

Portuguese Empire.summary: A changing network of colonies, trading posts and maritime routes spanning Africa, Asia and the Americas under Portuguese rule.
Portuguese Empire.capital: Lisbon for most of the period; Rio de Janeiro replaced it as the imperial capital in 1808–1821.
Portuguese Empire.currency: Real in metropolitan Portugal, replaced by the escudo in 1911; colonial currencies differed by territory.
Portuguese Empire.economy: Maritime commerce, African gold, plantation production and the slave trade supported imperial connections; slavery was central to Portuguese America.
Portuguese Empire.military: Fortified trading posts and overseas conquests supported maritime expansion; military capacity and control varied sharply between territories.
Portuguese Empire.contributions: Oceanic routes linked previously separate trading systems and generated lasting cultural exchanges alongside slavery and colonial violence.
Portuguese Empire.origin: The conquest of Ceuta in 1415 preceded Atlantic expansion and the establishment of overseas settlements and trading posts.
Portuguese Empire.decline: Decolonization accelerated after the 1974 revolution; Portugal recognized African colonial independence in 1974–1975 and ended its administration of Macao in 1999.
Portuguese Empire.periodNote: 1415 marks Ceuta’s conquest; 1999 marks the Macao handover. This umbrella record spans different regimes and does not imply uniformly controlled territory.

British Empire.summary: A changing system of British colonies, protectorates, dominions and other dependencies, governed through different degrees of direct and indirect control.
British Empire.capital: London, the metropolitan center of imperial government.
British Empire.currency: Pound sterling and numerous territorial currencies; imperial territories did not share one uniform monetary system.
British Empire.rulers: Selected monarch: Victoria, 1837–1901; policy was also directed by ministers, Parliament and colonial administrations.
British Empire.economy: Imperial commerce and colonial resources supported industrial growth; exploitation and coercion shaped the distribution of economic benefits.
British Empire.military: British forces and colonial armies secured territories and trade routes; losing access to the Indian Army weakened Britain’s global military capacity after 1947.
British Empire.origin: Merchant charters, Atlantic settlement and overseas conquest produced an expanding imperial system; Jamestown became a permanent English settlement in 1607.
British Empire.decline: Independence movements and postwar political change dismantled most colonial rule; Hong Kong’s transfer to China in 1997 became a symbolic endpoint.
British Empire.periodNote: 1607 begins this overseas-settlement convention; 1997 is a symbolic endpoint. Earlier English expansion preceded it, and British Overseas Territories remained afterward.

French Colonial Empire.summary: French colonies, protectorates and mandated territories formed through distinct waves of overseas expansion, with different systems of administration and citizenship.
French Colonial Empire.capital: Paris; Versailles was the principal royal seat of government from 1682 to 1789, with interruptions.
French Colonial Empire.currency: Currencies varied across territories; the CFA and CFP francs were created in 1945 within the colonial monetary system.
French Colonial Empire.rulers: Selected monarch: Louis XIV, 1643–1715. Later colonial rule continued under other monarchies and republics.
French Colonial Empire.economy: Caribbean plantation exports relied on enslaved labor; other territories supplied commodities and trading bases under changing colonial economic arrangements.
French Colonial Empire.military: French armed forces conducted colonial conquests, including Algeria from 1830 and extensive African campaigns during the late nineteenth century.
French Colonial Empire.contributions: Colonial encounters produced enduring cultural and linguistic exchanges while imposed rule and slavery reshaped colonized societies.
French Colonial Empire.origin: Commercial ventures, strategic rivalry and missionary objectives developed into state-directed overseas colonization.
French Colonial Empire.decline: Wars, independence movements and decolonization dismantled most imperial rule; Vanuatu’s independence ended the Anglo-French condominium in 1980.
French Colonial Empire.periodNote: 1534 marks Cartier’s first voyage; 1980 marks Vanuatu’s independence, not the disappearance of French overseas territories. First and second colonial empires are often studied separately.

Holy Roman Empire.summary: An elective imperial framework joining a changing collection of kingdoms, principalities, ecclesiastical territories and cities in central Europe.
Holy Roman Empire.military: Imperial estates contributed troops or money under negotiated obligations; imperial defense depended on cooperation among territorial rulers.
Holy Roman Empire.contributions: Imperial institutions provided a durable framework for political negotiation and legal order across fragmented central Europe.
Holy Roman Empire.origin: Otto I’s imperial coronation in Rome in 962 joined German royal power to renewed claims of Roman imperial authority.
Holy Roman Empire.decline: Napoleonic victories and political reorganization preceded Francis II’s abdication and dissolution of the empire in 1806.
Holy Roman Empire.periodNote: 962 follows the conventional chronology used by the German Historical Museum, beginning with Otto I’s imperial coronation. It describes this empire, rather than all earlier claims to Roman imperial succession.

Russian Empire.summary: The Russian monarchy after adoption of the imperial title, expanding and governing territories across Europe, the Caucasus and northern and central Asia.
Russian Empire.capital: Saint Petersburg for most of the imperial period.
Russian Empire.currency: Ruble, divided into 100 kopeks after Peter I’s monetary reforms.
Russian Empire.rulers: Selected rulers: Peter I, emperor 1721–1725; Catherine II, 1762–1796.
Russian Empire.economy: Peter’s military reforms stimulated industry and reorganized fiscal administration; economic conditions changed substantially over the empire’s two centuries.
Russian Empire.military: The Great Northern War drove army reform and Baltic expansion; subsequent rulers pursued further territorial enlargement.
Russian Empire.contributions: Imperial patronage developed major artistic collections and institutions, notably Catherine II’s collection that became the Hermitage.
Russian Empire.origin: Peter adopted the imperial title after victory in the Great Northern War in 1721.
Russian Empire.decline: The 1917 revolution overthrew the monarchy, ending imperial government and initiating contested successor regimes.
Russian Empire.periodNote: 1721 marks adoption of the imperial title, not the beginning of the Russian state. Monarchical rule ended in March 1917.

Soviet Union.summary: A formally federal socialist state governed by the Communist Party that became a major industrial, military and diplomatic power.
Soviet Union.currency: Soviet ruble; chervonets-denominated banknotes also circulated before the 1947 monetary reform.
Soviet Union.rulers: Selected leader: Mikhail Gorbachev, 1985–1991; Communist Party general secretary until August 1991 and USSR president until December 1991.
Soviet Union.economy: State ownership and central planning dominated much of its history; forced industrialization and collectivization transformed production at enormous human cost.
Soviet Union.military: A nuclear superpower with large conventional forces, competing with the United States during the Cold War.
Soviet Union.contributions: Launched the first artificial satellite, Sputnik 1, in 1957 and the first human into space, Yuri Gagarin, in 1961.
Soviet Union.origin: Bolshevik victory in civil war preceded the union of Russia, Ukraine, Belarus and the Transcaucasian federation in December 1922.
Soviet Union.decline: Economic crisis, political reforms, republican independence movements and the failed August 1991 coup culminated in dissolution.
Soviet Union.periodNote: 1922 marks formation of the USSR, distinct from the Bolshevik seizure of power in 1917. It dissolved in December 1991; it was formally a union, not a monarchy.

Aztec Empire.summary: A tributary alliance led by Tenochtitlan that dominated much of central and southern Mexico while many subject communities retained local rulers.
Aztec Empire.capital: Tenochtitlan was the dominant center; Texcoco and Tlacopan were the other Triple Alliance partners.
Aztec Empire.currency: Cacao beans served as a medium of exchange; they were not a standardized minted coinage.
Aztec Empire.rulers: Selected rulers of Tenochtitlan: Motecuhzoma I, 1440–1469; Ahuitzotl, 1486–1502; Motecuhzoma II, 1502–1520.
Aztec Empire.economy: Tribute, agriculture and interregional trade supplied the capital with staples, labor and luxury goods.
Aztec Empire.military: Conquest armies expanded tribute obligations, but independent rivals, including Tlaxcala and the Tarascan state, resisted imperial domination.
Aztec Empire.contributions: Monumental sculpture, urban ceremonial architecture and specialized crafts developed within a densely connected tributary society.
Aztec Empire.origin: Tenochtitlan allied with Texcoco and Tlacopan to defeat Azcapotzalco and establish regional dominance.
Aztec Empire.decline: Spanish forces and Indigenous allies, including Tlaxcala, conquered Tenochtitlan in 1521; disease and colonial exploitation devastated populations.
Aztec Empire.periodNote: The Triple Alliance is commonly dated 1428; The Met gives approximately 1427. The earlier city-state and the imperial alliance have different starting dates.

Inca Empire.summary: An Andean imperial state centered on Cusco that integrated diverse communities through administration, labor obligations, roads and regional redistribution.
Inca Empire.currency: No widespread coined currency; state obligations were principally organized around labor.
Inca Empire.rulers: Selected ruler: Pachakuti, conventionally c. 1438–1471; early Inca reign dates are reconstructed from later accounts.
Inca Empire.economy: Households supplied labor taxes; agricultural production, storage and redistribution supported state projects and armies.
Inca Empire.military: Inca rulers conquered neighboring territories from the fifteenth century, integrating extensive Andean regions.
Inca Empire.contributions: An extensive road network and sophisticated water engineering connected and sustained communities across difficult Andean terrain.
Inca Empire.origin: A Cusco-based kingdom began large-scale territorial expansion under Pachakuti around 1438.
Inca Empire.decline: Epidemics and succession war weakened imperial authority before Spanish invasion, Atahualpa’s capture and execution, and the occupation of Cusco.
Inca Empire.periodNote: 1438 marks imperial expansion; 1533 marks the conquest phase that ended the main imperial government. A successor Inca state at Vilcabamba resisted until 1572.
